Q137911647.summary: Under a round-headed arch, the dead Christ is lowered from the cross: one figure supports his body while another, kneeling, draws the nail from his feet, and mourners stand at either side, with further figures above the cross. The small carving gathers the grief and tenderness of the moment into a tight, devotional composition.
facts: Wikidata records the relief as pearwood, about 26.7 cm high, in the Bode-Museum's Romanesque sculpture collection.
Q137911647.notes: Only Wikidata and Commons were available (the museum's online database was down). The Commons file name links the relief to Trier, which could not be confirmed. The identity of the mourners is not certain from the photograph.

cur:catacombs-three-shepherds-sarcophagu.summary: Three shepherds carrying sheep stand on pedestals at the ends and centre, while the whole surface between them is filled with vines in which winged putti harvest and tread the grapes. The vintage, a symbol of the Eucharist and of paradise, surrounds the Good Shepherd, the image of Christ caring for the souls of the dead.
facts: The sarcophagus is displayed in the Museo Pio Cristiano and dated by Commons to the second half of the 4th century.
The motif of the grape harvest by putti was shared with pagan Dionysiac art and given new meaning in Christian use.
cur:catacombs-three-shepherds-sarcophagu.notes: The Good Shepherd figures are symbolic; their identification with Christ is an interpretation, well established in this Christian context.

cur:manuscripts-lorsch-gospels-christ-ab.summary: Above the arcade framing the gold-lettered preface to Matthew's Gospel, a lunette is filled with crowds of figures arranged in tiers, with framed busts among them; at the very top, in a blue medallion, Christ sits enthroned. The composition visualises Matthew's genealogy, with the generations of Christ's ancestors leading up to him.
facts: The Lorsch Gospels takes its name from Lorsch Abbey, for which it was probably made; it is also called the Codex Aureus because it is written entirely in gold ink.
According to German Wikipedia, the book contained four evangelist portraits and a Majestas Domini, twelve canon tables and prefaces to each Gospel.
cur:manuscripts-lorsch-gospels-christ-ab.notes: Folio not given by the Commons source. Identification of the tiers of figures as Christ's ancestors follows the Matthew prologue (Argumentum) that the page introduces.

cur:monumental-san-paralytic-bethesda.summary: The healed man strides away with his bed strapped to his back while Christ, haloed in purple and followed by a disciple, raises his hand in blessing and command. The mosaicists showed the moment just after the miracle, when Christ's word 'Rise, take up thy bed, and walk' has already done its work.
facts: The thirteen scenes of the north wall show Christ's miracles and teaching; in all of them he appears young and beardless, robed in imperial purple.
The cycle contains two healings of paralytics: this one at the pool of Bethesda, and another at Capernaum in which the sick man is let down through the roof.
The scenes were not arranged in biblical order but are thought to follow the Gospel readings of the Lenten liturgy in Theodoric's palace church.

cur:monumental2-tokali-last-supper.summary: Christ, haloed and robed in blue, reclines at the left end of a semicircular table while the apostles crowd in a curving row behind it; a single large red chalice-like dish stands at the centre of the green tabletop. The scene belongs to the Passion register of the Old Church's barrel-vault cycle, painted in the pale reds and greens that distinguish the Old Church from the later, blue New Church.
facts: The Old Church vault carries one of the fullest Christological cycles in Cappadocia: on each side three registers show the Infancy, the Miracles and the Passion, with a spine of prophet medallions along the crown of the vault.
The sigma-shaped (semicircular) table with Christ reclining at one end follows the ancient banqueting arrangement used in early Christian and Byzantine images of the Last Supper.
